(CNN) -- Thousands of Chileans may have to sleep in the streets Wednesday night after a 7.7 magnitude earthquake rattled the north part of the country, killing at least two people, injuring dozens and destroying hundreds of homes. Valentina Bustos shot this photo Wednesday  of earthquake damage at a hotel in Antofagasta, Chile. "There are more than a thousand, 1,200 houses, at least, that were totally flattened, and others in bad shape," Tocopilla Mayor Luis Moyano said in an interview that aired on Radio Cooperativo. Tocopilla, Chile, north of Santiago, is about 35 km (21 miles) from the quake's epicenter. "Tonight, people are going to have to sleep in the street, because there are a great number of houses that are uninhabitable," said Moyano. Places that could be used as shelters, such as schools and gyms, were  damaged in the quake, the mayor said. Moyano put the number of people without shelter at 4,000. Tocopilla's population is 24,000. Moyano described going through the damaged city and running into people asking, "Mayor, my house collapsed. What do I do? Mayor, I don't have water. What do I do?" "It gets to you," he said. Paula Saez with the aid organization World Vision told CNN she was on a treacherous drive attempting to reach Tocopilla. "There's no electricity and there's a lot of landslides" covering the road in spots, she said, and the highway was spotted with holes. Once in Tocopilla, Saez said, she was prepared to offer tents, blankets and medicine to citizens and assess additional needs. The government's Office of National Emergency reported that two women had died and others were injured in the city. Officials identified one of those killed as 54-year-old Olga Petronila Ortiz Cisternas. The other fatality was an 88-year-old woman.  Watch what a 7.7 earthquake can do » . Municipal official Ljubica Ukurtovic, in an interview with Chilean TV station TVN, said that "approximately 100 people" had sought treatment at a Tocopilla hospital. The quake collapsed a roadway tunnel, temporarily trapping about 50 construction workers.  See where the quake struck » . High-level government sources said the workers had been rescued. Repair work on the 793-meter (2,600-foot) Pedro Galleguillos tunnel, completed in 1994, began on October 1 and was to be finished early next year. Tocopilla is about 1,245 km (780 miles) north of Santiago and the quake was felt in Peru and Bolivia, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. The temblor was centered at a depth of 60 km (37 miles), the USGS said. A tsunami warning was issued for the South Pacific coast after the quake hit, but was canceled within an hour. Chile has been the scene of hundreds of strong earthquakes throughout history, including the largest one of the 20th century on May 22, 1960. The quake that struck southern Chile that day registered a magnitude 9.5 and launched a tsunami that caused damage as far away as Hawaii, Japan and the Philippines. Nearly 6,000 people died as a result of the quake and its tsunami. A magnitude 7.8 earthquake that struck southern Chile on January 25, 1939, killed 28,000 people. A magnitude 9.0 earthquake in what was then southern Peru but is now northern Chile killed 25,000 people in 1868.  E-mail to a friend .

(CNN) — A powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake shook northern Chile on Wednesday, leaving at least two people dead, dozens hurt and hundreds of homes destroyed. As a result, thousands of residents may be forced to spend Wednesday night outdoors.

Valentina Bustos took a photograph Wednesday showing quake damage at a hotel in Antofagasta, Chile.

Tocopilla Mayor Luis Moyano told Radio Cooperativo that at least 1,200 homes had been completely leveled, with many others seriously damaged. Tocopilla, located north of Santiago, lies about 35 kilometers, or 21 miles, from the earthquake’s epicenter.

“Tonight, people are going to have to sleep in the street,” Moyano said, explaining that many homes could no longer be lived in. He added that possible emergency shelters, including schools and gymnasiums, had also suffered damage. According to Moyano, about 4,000 people were left without shelter in the city, which has a population of roughly 24,000.

The mayor said that as he moved through the devastated city, residents approached him with urgent questions such as, “Mayor, my house collapsed. What do I do?” and “Mayor, I don’t have water. What do I do?” He said the situation was emotionally overwhelming.

Paula Saez of the aid group World Vision told CNN she was making a difficult trip to Tocopilla. She said the area had no power, roads were blocked in places by numerous landslides, and the highway was damaged by holes. Saez said that once she arrived, she planned to provide residents with tents, blankets and medicine, while also evaluating what further assistance was needed.

Chile’s Office of National Emergency said two women had died and other people had been injured in Tocopilla. Authorities named one victim as 54-year-old Olga Petronila Ortiz Cisternas. The second person killed was an 88-year-old woman.

Ljubica Ukurtovic, a municipal official, told Chilean television station TVN that around 100 people had gone to a Tocopilla hospital for medical care.

The earthquake also caused a roadway tunnel to collapse, briefly trapping about 50 construction workers. Senior government officials later said the workers had been rescued. The 793-meter, or 2,600-foot, Pedro Galleguillos tunnel, completed in 1994, had been undergoing repairs since October 1, with the work expected to finish early the following year.

Tocopilla is approximately 1,245 kilometers, or 780 miles, north of Santiago. The U.S. Geological Survey reported that the quake was felt in Peru and Bolivia. According to the USGS, the earthquake originated 60 kilometers, or 37 miles, below the surface.

A tsunami warning was issued for the South Pacific coast after the earthquake, but it was withdrawn within an hour.

Chile has experienced hundreds of major earthquakes over the course of its history. Among them was the strongest quake of the 20th century, which struck southern Chile on May 22, 1960. That earthquake measured 9.5 in magnitude and triggered a tsunami that caused damage as far away as Hawaii, Japan and the Philippines. Nearly 6,000 people died from the quake and tsunami.

Other deadly earthquakes in the region include a 7.8-magnitude quake in southern Chile on January 25, 1939, which killed 28,000 people, and a magnitude 9.0 quake in 1868 in what was then southern Peru and is now northern Chile, which left 25,000 dead.

# Major 7.7-Magnitude Earthquake Strikes Northern Chile Near Tocopilla, Prompting Tsunami Warning and Emergency Response

**SANTIAGO, Chile —** A powerful **7.7-magnitude earthquake** struck off the coast of **northern Chile near Tocopilla** on Monday, shaking cities across the Antofagasta region, damaging buildings and roads, and prompting authorities to issue a precautionary **tsunami warning** for parts of the Chilean coastline.

The quake hit at a shallow-to-moderate depth offshore, according to preliminary seismic data, sending residents rushing into streets as strong shaking was reported in **Tocopilla, Calama, Mejillones and Antofagasta**. Tremors were also felt in parts of southern Peru and western Bolivia, local media reported.

Chilean emergency officials said early reports indicated **at least several deaths and dozens of injuries**, though they cautioned that casualty figures were expected to change as rescue crews reached harder-hit communities and communication was restored.

## Damage Reported in Coastal Towns

In Tocopilla, a port city with a history of earthquake damage, local officials reported collapsed walls, cracked roads, power outages and damage to older buildings. Images from the area showed debris scattered across streets, broken storefront windows and residents gathered in open spaces away from buildings.

Hospitals in the region were operating under emergency protocols, with some patients being moved to safer areas as aftershocks continued.

“The priority right now is saving lives, restoring communications and ensuring people are moved away from coastal risk zones,” a regional emergency official said at a late-night briefing.

Authorities said several highways in the Antofagasta region were being inspected for landslides and structural damage, and mining operations in the region — a major hub for Chile’s copper industry — temporarily paused activity while safety assessments were conducted.

## Tsunami Warning Issued

Chile’s navy hydrographic and oceanographic service issued a **tsunami warning** shortly after the quake, ordering evacuations from low-lying coastal areas near the epicenter. Sirens sounded in multiple coastal communities as emergency messages urged residents to move to higher ground.

“People in designated evacuation zones should not return to the coast until authorities confirm it is safe,” an emergency management spokesperson said.

The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center said hazardous tsunami waves were possible near the Chilean coast and that monitoring would continue. Officials emphasized that even small tsunami waves can create strong currents and dangerous coastal conditions.

## Shelters Opened as Aftershocks Continue

The government said temporary shelters were being opened in schools, sports centers and municipal buildings for residents whose homes were damaged or who were evacuated from coastal neighborhoods.

Emergency managers said the most urgent needs included:

- **Safe shelter for displaced families**
- **Drinking water**
- **Blankets and warm clothing**
- **Medical supplies**
- **Generators and fuel**
- **Food and infant supplies**
- **Satellite communications equipment**

Aftershocks, some of them strong, continued to rattle the region in the hours after the main quake, complicating rescue and inspection efforts.

## National Aid Response Mobilized

Chile’s government said it had activated national disaster response protocols and deployed military units, firefighters, police and medical teams to affected areas. Search-and-rescue crews were sent to Tocopilla and nearby communities to inspect collapsed structures and assist trapped residents.

President **Gabriel Boric** said the government was coordinating with regional authorities and urged the public to follow evacuation orders.

“We know the people of northern Chile are accustomed to earthquakes, but this is a serious event,” Boric said. “Our focus is on protecting lives, reaching isolated communities and providing immediate support to families who have lost their homes.”

The Interior Ministry said aerial surveys would begin at first light to assess damage along the coast and in remote desert communities.

International aid organizations also said they were monitoring the situation and preparing to support local responders if requested. Neighboring countries offered technical assistance, including emergency communications and medical support.

## A Region Familiar With Powerful Quakes

Chile lies along the **Pacific Ring of Fire**, one of the most seismically active regions in the world, where the Nazca Plate dives beneath the South American Plate. The country has experienced some of the strongest earthquakes ever recorded.

The most powerful known earthquake in modern history — a **9.5-magnitude quake** — struck southern Chile in 1960, generating a devastating Pacific-wide tsunami. In 2010, an **8.8-magnitude earthquake** hit central Chile, killing more than 500 people and causing widespread destruction.

Northern Chile has also endured major seismic events, including powerful quakes near Iquique and Antofagasta. Tocopilla itself was struck by a damaging earthquake in 2007, which caused deaths, injuries and significant structural damage.

Experts say strict building codes have helped reduce casualties in Chile compared with other earthquake-prone countries, but older homes, informal construction and coastal tsunami exposure remain significant risks.

## Authorities Urge Caution

Officials warned residents not to re-enter damaged buildings, approach the shoreline or spread unverified information. Emergency agencies said updates would be issued as casualty figures, damage reports and tsunami assessments become clearer.

“This remains an active emergency,” authorities said. “Stay on high ground if you are in an evacuation zone, check on neighbors where it is safe to do so, and wait for official instructions.”

Chile’s emergency services said the full extent of the damage could take time to assess because communications were disrupted in some areas.

The quake did not immediately generate a major tsunami threat, but coastal communities remained on edge because of Chile’s long history of devastating seismic events.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an Associated Press/CNN-like disaster news story covering a major earthquake in northern Chile, including the epicenter near Tocopilla, rescue of construction workers from the Pedro Galleguillos tunnel, emergency response, and comparisons to historic Chilean quakes.
counterfactuals.output:
**Major earthquake strikes northern Chile; workers rescued from tunnel near Tocopilla**

**SANTIAGO, Chile (AP/CNN)** — A powerful earthquake struck northern Chile, shaking desert communities along the Pacific coast, damaging roads and buildings, and triggering emergency operations around the mining and construction corridors near Tocopilla, officials said.

The quake’s epicenter was reported near **Tocopilla**, a port city in the Antofagasta region, an area accustomed to seismic activity but still vulnerable to landslides, power outages and damage to older structures. Strong shaking was felt across parts of northern Chile, including Antofagasta, Calama and coastal towns along the Atacama Desert.

Authorities said emergency crews were dispatched shortly after the quake to assess damage, clear blocked roads and inspect critical infrastructure, including hospitals, ports, mines and power facilities. Chile’s national disaster response agency activated regional emergency protocols, while local officials urged residents to remain away from damaged buildings and to be prepared for aftershocks.

One of the most urgent operations unfolded at the **Pedro Galleguillos tunnel**, where a group of construction workers was trapped after rockfalls and structural damage blocked access. Rescue teams, supported by firefighters, police, engineers and heavy equipment operators, worked for hours to stabilize the area and open a passage into the tunnel.

Officials later confirmed that the workers had been reached and brought out alive, prompting cheers from relatives and rescue crews gathered near the site. Some of the workers were treated for dehydration, shock and minor injuries, authorities said.

“Chile knows how to respond to earthquakes, but every rescue is a race against time,” a regional emergency official said. “The priority has been saving lives, restoring communications and making sure communities remain supplied.”

Hospitals in the affected region reported treating residents for injuries related to falling debris, broken glass and panic during evacuations. Power and cellphone service were disrupted in several communities, complicating early damage assessments. Crews also inspected highways carved through steep desert terrain, where landslides and cracked pavement were reported.

No nationwide tsunami alert was immediately in effect, though coastal authorities advised residents to follow official guidance and avoid beaches until maritime conditions were fully evaluated.

Chile lies along the so-called **Ring of Fire**, where the Nazca tectonic plate dives beneath the South American plate, producing some of the world’s strongest earthquakes. The country has invested heavily in seismic-resistant construction and emergency planning, but its long coastline and mountainous terrain make rapid response difficult in remote areas.

The latest quake drew immediate comparisons to Chile’s most destructive seismic events, including the **1960 Valdivia earthquake**, the strongest ever recorded at magnitude 9.5, and the **2010 Maule earthquake**, a magnitude 8.8 disaster that triggered a tsunami and killed hundreds. Northern Chile has also endured major quakes, including powerful events near Iquique and Antofagasta, underscoring the persistent risk in the region.

President and regional authorities were expected to travel to the affected area as daylight allowed fuller inspections. Officials said damage assessments would continue through the night and warned that strong aftershocks could follow.

“For Chileans, earthquakes are part of our history,” one Tocopilla resident said after leaving her damaged home. “But when the ground moves like that, you never get used to it.”
